query: Given that refractory high-entropy alloys containing Group IV elements are highly susceptible to embrittlement via oxygen uptake during processing, leading to the precipitation of brittle alpha-HCP phases that raise the transition temperature, how can a powder-based extrusion method be adapted to manage oxygen content during the thermal decomposition of hydride precursors? Specifically, what thermal history and environmental constraints are required to achieve a dense bulk form without catastrophic cracking, and how can the formation of metastable phases be controlled to maximize high-temperature yield strength?

generation.hypothesis: A powder-based extrusion method utilizing hydride precursors for refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) containing Group IV elements can achieve dense bulk forms without catastrophic cracking by employing a controlled thermal decomposition profile under ultra-high vacuum (<10^-5 Pa) or inert gas (Ar) with oxygen scavengers, followed by hot extrusion at temperatures just below the alpha-HCP phase formation threshold. This approach minimizes oxygen uptake during precursor decomposition, suppresses brittle alpha-HCP precipitation, and retains a metastable BCC solid solution, thereby maximizing high-temperature yield strength while avoiding transition temperature elevation.
generation.material_initial_state: Powder mixture of Group IV-containing refractory high-entropy alloy precursors (e.g., Hf, Zr, Ti) in hydride form (e.g., HfH2, ZrH2, TiH2) with controlled particle size distribution, prepared under inert atmosphere to minimize initial oxygen content.
generation.intervention: Thermal decomposition of hydride precursors in a vacuum/inert environment at a controlled heating rate (e.g., 5-10 °C/min) to a peak temperature of 800-1000 °C to release hydrogen without oxidizing the alloy, followed by immediate consolidation via hot extrusion at 1100-1300 °C under high pressure (200-400 MPa) to achieve full density.
generation.conditions: Atmosphere: Ultra-high vacuum (<10^-5 Pa) or high-purity argon with oxygen scavengers (e.g., Ti, Zr getters). Temperature: Decomposition at 800-1000 °C; Extrusion at 1100-1300 °C. Pressure: 200-400 MPa during extrusion. Time: Short dwell times (<10 min) to limit oxygen diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: Metastable body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution phase, stabilized by rapid cooling and low oxygen content, preventing the nucleation of brittle alpha-HCP phases.
generation.mechanism: Controlled thermal decomposition of hydrides releases hydrogen without introducing oxygen, while the low-oxygen environment and rapid consolidation prevent the formation of brittle oxide precipitates and alpha-HCP phases. The BCC structure is retained due to suppressed oxygen diffusion and phase transformation kinetics, leading to enhanced high-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Dense bulk RHEA with minimal porosity (<1%), no catastrophic cracking, suppressed alpha-HCP phase formation, and significantly improved high-temperature yield strength (e.g., >1500 MPa at 1000 °C) compared to conventionally processed alloys.
generation.baseline: Conventionally processed RHEAs via arc melting or spark plasma sintering, which often exhibit high oxygen content, alpha-HCP precipitation, and brittle fracture due to oxygen embrittlement.
generation.boundary: Applicable to RHEAs with Group IV elements (Hf, Zr, Ti) and refractory metals (Nb, Ta, W, Mo, V). Not suitable for alloys with high oxygen affinity elements that cannot be scavenged effectively.
generation.uncertainty: The exact decomposition kinetics of mixed hydride precursors and the precise oxygen scavenging efficiency in large-scale extrusion processes are not fully characterized. Variations in precursor purity and particle size may affect the reproducibility of the process.
generation.falsification_experiment: Perform extrusion of Group IV-containing RHEA hydride precursors under varying oxygen levels (10^-3 Pa to 10^-6 Pa) and measure the resulting alpha-HCP phase fraction via XRD and TEM. If alpha-HCP phases form even at ultra-high vacuum levels, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract A NbMoTaWVTi refractory high entropy alloy (HEA) has been successfully synthesized by mechanical alloying (MA) and spark plasma sintering (SPS). The microstructure and mechanical properties of this alloy are investigated. It is observed that only two types of body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solutions are formed in the powders after ball milling for 40 h. However, a new face-centered cubic (FCC) precipitated phase is observed in the BCC matrix of bulk material consolidated by SPS. The FCC precipitated phase is identified as TiO, due to the introduction of O during the preparing process of HEA. The compressive yield strength, fracture strength, and total fracture strain of the consolidated bulk HEA are 2709 MPa, 3115 MPa, and 11.4%, respectively. The excellent mechanical properties can be attributed to solid solution strengthening and grain boundary strengthening of the fine-grained BCC matrix, as well as the precipitation strengthening owing to the formation of TiO particles. Keywords: refractory high entropy alloy, microstructure, mechanical properties

According to the traditional alloy design theory, ordered phases or intermetallic compounds will form as the number of alloying elements increases. However, Yeh et al. observes that simple solid solution phases, instead of intermetallic compounds, are formed in an equiatomic quinary alloy. Subsequently, they propose a new alloy system, termed high entropy alloys (HEAs), which contain at least five principal elements, each having the atomic percentage between 5% and 35% [ [1] , [2] ]. Since the development of HEAs, a substantial number of studies on HEA have been performed. Some of these studies are focused on alloys comprised of elements with low melting points, such as AlCoCrCuFeNi system alloys [ [3] , [4] ], commonly exhibiting high ductility and low strength. On the other hand, refractory HEAs have exhibited advantages of high yield strength at room and elevated temperature. For example, Nb25Mo25Ta25W25 and V20Nb20Mo20Ta20 refractory HEAs produced by vacuum arc-melting exhibit compressive yield strengths of 1058 MPa and 1246 MPa, respectively, with plasticities of less than 2% at room temperature [ [5] ]. Abstract High entropy alloys (HEA) have been one of the most attractive groups of materials for researchers in the last several years. Since HEAs are potential candidates for many (e.g., refractory, cryogenic, medical) applications, their properties are studied intensively. The most frequent method of HEA synthesis is arc or induction melting. Powder metallurgy is a perspective technique of alloy synthesis and therefore in this work the possibilities of synthesis of HfNbTaTiZr HEA from powders were studied. Blended elemental powders were sintered, hot isostatically pressed, and subsequently swaged using a special technique of swaging where the sample is enveloped by a titanium alloy. This method does not result in a full density alloy due to cracking during swaging. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed powders resulted in a fully dense but brittle specimen. The most promising result was obtained by SPS treatment of gas atomized powder with low oxygen content. Results obtained for HEAP-S and HEAP-S-HIP samples (see Table 2 ) indicate that HIP processing had some potential to decrease residual porosity. However, this decrease was quite small and considerable porosity remained in the specimen. The fact that even HIP processing at 1400 °C/200 MPa/2 h did not remove the porosity completely can be ascribed to a high volume fraction of pores and to filling of the pores by Ar gas used as a pressing medium in HIP processing. The MA powder compacted by SPS contained residual porosity as well, and small pores remained in the sample even after HPT processing, as seen in Figure 6 . It should be pointed out that the MA-SPS-HPT specimen was broken into several pieces during the HPT process and therefore the results of such specimen are disputable. In such cases, the HPT after cracking could not introduce full deformation (strain) to the specimen. Contrary to this, SPS processing at 1300 °C of AT powder resulted in porosity-free samples (see Figure 7 ).
